57.title: The switched bride (Genesis 29:21–30)
57.hook: the trickster is tricked, and wakes to find Leah instead of Rachel
57.howItsDone: Jews read the switched bride in the Torah portion Vayetze; one explanation given for the bedeken, when the groom lowers the bride's veil himself so he can see her face, points back to this story.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Rachel, and seven years that seemed but a few days, for Jacob's love. A new week starts here.

Seven years are up. Jacob goes to Laban: give me my wife, my time is done. Laban throws a great wedding feast and invites every man in the place. There's food, there's drink. In the evening, Laban takes his daughter and brings her to Jacob. The Torah doesn't stop to explain how Jacob didn't know. It just waits for daylight. And the next verse, in the old JPS translation, lands like a slap: "And it came to pass in the morning that, behold, it was Leah." Not Rachel. Her older sister. After seven years of work, after all that love, Jacob wakes up to the wrong face. The trickster, tricked.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS ARE UP.` → `A FEAST, THEN EVENING.` → `BEHOLD, IT WAS LEAH.`

segments.voice: Jacob storms to Laban: "What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban answers, calm as anything: "It is not so done in our place, to give the younger before the first-born." The younger before the firstborn. That is exactly what Jacob did to Esau. Before a father whose eyes were too dim to see, Jacob, the younger, put himself in place of the firstborn. Now, in the night, the firstborn is put in place of the younger, and Jacob is the one who can't see. A word ties the two stories together. When Jacob asks why Laban beguiled him, the Hebrew is from the root of mirmah, deceit, the same root Isaac used to Esau: "Thy brother came with guile, and hath taken away thy blessing." The Torah doesn't have to say it's payback. It just uses the same root. A midrash imagines the morning after. Jacob says to Leah: all night I called you Rachel, and you answered. Leah says: your father called you Esau, and you answered. The rabbis had a name for this pattern: measure for measure. What you do has a way of coming back around. But notice Leah too, standing in the middle of two men's deals, married to someone who wanted her sister. Laban lets Jacob finish the wedding week, then gives him Rachel as well, for another seven years of work. Jacob now has two wives, sisters, and a house built on a trick. Tomorrow, Leah's side.

58.title: Leah's sons (Genesis 29:31–35)
58.hook: the unloved sister names each son for a hope, and at Judah simply praises
58.howItsDone: Jewish tradition begins the morning with Modeh Ani, a short prayer of thanks said on waking, from the same Hebrew root as Judah's name; the word Jew itself comes from Judah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mirmah, deceit, the same root in two stories, and the trickster tricked. Today, Leah's side.

Put yourself in Leah's place. You were married off in the dark, as a trick. Your husband woke up angry to see your face. A week later he married your younger sister, the one he really wanted. You live in the same camp, and everyone knows. The Torah says it plainly: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. Then, in the old JPS translation: "And the LORD saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb." Hated there means loved less, passed over. Nobody in the family seems to see her. But God sees her. And Leah, the sister nobody chose, starts to have children, and gives each one a name that says exactly what's in her heart.
screen: `MARRIED IN THE DARK.` → `LOVED LESS THAN HER SISTER.` → `THE LORD SAW LEAH.`

segments.voice: Her first son is Reuben. The name sounds like see, a son, and Leah explains it: God has seen my suffering; now my husband will love me. The second is Simeon, from the word for hearing: God has heard that I am unloved. The third is Levi, from the word for joining: this time my husband will be joined to me. Seen. Heard. Joined. Every name is a hope, and every hope is about Jacob. Maybe this baby will make him love me. And this one. And this one. It's the tiredness of trying to earn someone's love. Then comes the fourth son, and this time the name is different. "This time will I praise the LORD." She calls him Judah, Yehudah, from the Hebrew for thanks and praise. No mention of Jacob, or of what she still doesn't have. Just praise. The Talmud says something startling about this moment: from the day God created the world, no one had ever thanked God, until Leah came and said, this time I will praise. And the story reaches all the way to today. From Judah comes the tribe of Judah, and from Judah comes the word Jew. The very name of the Jewish people carries Leah's thank-you inside it. The same root opens the short prayer said on waking in Jewish tradition: modeh ani, I give thanks. The unloved sister named the people. And in the end, it's Leah, not Rachel, who is buried beside Jacob.

If you pray, you can offer that thanks as your prayer.

Your line: this time, praise. Three hopes for love, then one plain thank-you. See you tomorrow.

59.title: Rachel's longing (Genesis 30:1–24)
59.hook: years of waiting, then Joseph; the family grows through rivalry and prayer
59.howItsDone: Jews read Rachel's story in the Torah portion Vayetze and hear Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping on Rosh Hashanah; many people, especially women hoping for children, visit Rachel's Tomb near Bethlehem to pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Leah's sons, named seen, heard and joined, and then Judah: this time, praise.

Rachel is the loved one. Jacob worked fourteen years for her. She watches her sister have one son, then two, three, four. She has none. The Torah doesn't make her gracious about it: she envied her sister. She goes to Jacob and says, in the old JPS translation: "Give me children, or else I die." It's one of the rawest sentences in Genesis. Anyone who has waited for a child, or for anything everyone around them seems to get easily, knows that voice. Jacob, who loves her, snaps: "Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?" Two people who love each other, both in pain, saying the wrong thing.
screen: `THE LOVED ONE, WITH NO CHILD.` → `GIVE ME CHILDREN, OR ELSE I DIE.` → `AM I IN GOD'S STEAD?`

segments.voice: What follows is messy, and the Torah tells it straight. Rachel gives Jacob her servant Bilhah, and names Bilhah's sons herself. One she calls Naphtali, from wrestling: I have wrestled mightily with my sister, and I have prevailed. Leah answers with her own servant, and more sons. The sisters even bargain over mandrakes, a plant people believed helped with fertility. Rivalry, out in the open. Then, at last: "And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb." She has a son and names him Joseph, Yosef, may He add: may God add another son to me. Even her joy has longing in it. But the rabbis saw more in Rachel than rivalry. The Talmud tells that before the wedding, Jacob and Rachel had agreed on secret signs, so Laban couldn't switch the bride. When Rachel saw Leah led to the tent, she gave Leah the signs, so Leah wouldn't be shamed. She gave away her own wedding night to protect her sister. A midrash tells that centuries later, when Jerusalem fell and the patriarchs pleaded with God for their children, God was silent, until Rachel spoke: I overcame my jealousy of my sister. God answered her. The prophet Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted, and God telling her to hold back her tears, for there is hope. Rachel wanted honestly, fought honestly, gave generously, and prayed. The tradition doesn't ask her to pretend. Her longing is part of why she's heard.

60.title: Leaving Laban (Genesis 31)
60.hook: twenty hard years, stolen idols, and a heap of stones as a boundary of peace
60.howItsDone: Jews read Jacob's departure from Laban in the Torah portion Vayetze; Laban's words at the heap give the place a second name, Mizpah, the watchpost (Genesis 31:49).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rachel's longing, said out loud, and at last Joseph, may He add.

Twenty years in Laban's house, and the mood has turned. Jacob came with a walking stick; now he has two wives, eleven sons, a daughter and huge flocks. Laban's sons grumble that Jacob got rich off their father. Laban's face, the Torah says, isn't toward him as it used to be. The welcome has quietly run out. Then God speaks: go back to the land of your fathers, and I will be with you. Jacob calls Rachel and Leah out to the field. And the two sisters, rivals until now, speak with one voice: our father has treated us like strangers. Whatever God told you, do it.
screen: `TWENTY YEARS IN LABAN'S HOUSE.` → `THE WELCOME HAS RUN OUT.` → `THE SISTERS SPEAK AS ONE.`

segments.voice: While Laban is away shearing sheep, Jacob loads everything onto camels and slips away. Rachel, without telling him, takes her father's household idols. Laban chases them for seven days and catches up in the hills of Gilead, but God has warned him in a dream: be careful what you say to Jacob. Rachel has hidden them in her camel's saddle; when Laban searches every tent for his stolen gods, she sits on them and apologizes that she can't get up. So the household gods, the kind Abram walked away from long ago, end up sat on. Rashi, the medieval commentator, says she took them to pull her father away from idol worship. Then Jacob lets out twenty years of anger, in the old JPS translation: "in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep fled from mine eyes." You changed my wages ten times, he says. But the story doesn't end in a fight. It ends in a pile of stones. Jacob sets up a pillar, the family heaps stones, and they eat there by the heap. Laban names it in Aramaic, Jegar-sahadutha; Jacob names it in Hebrew, Galeed. Two languages, one meaning: a heap of witness. Laban adds: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." The heap is a line. I won't cross it to harm you, and you won't cross it to harm me. Not friendship. Not love. A boundary, set in stone, so that peace can hold.

61.title: Wrestling at the river (Genesis 32:23–33)
61.hook: Jacob wrestles until dawn and is renamed Israel, one who strives with God
61.howItsDone: Observant Jews keep the Torah's rule not to eat the sciatic nerve, the gid hanasheh, which Genesis 32:33 ties to Jacob's limp; some readers also hear in the name Israel a permission to question and argue with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: leaving Laban, and a heap of witness between two men who didn't trust each other.

Esau is coming, with four hundred men. Free of Laban, Jacob is walking straight toward the other person he never settled with: the brother whose blessing he took before he ran. When the scouts bring the news, Jacob splits his camp in two, so if one half is attacked the other can run. He sends gifts ahead, herd after herd. At night, he sends his wives and children across the river Jabbok, with everything he owns. "And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day." No warning, no name: a fight in the dark that lasts all night.
screen: `ESAU IS COMING, WITH FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `JACOB, ALONE AT THE RIVER.` → `A FIGHT UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: The stranger can't win, so he touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh and puts it out of joint. It's getting light, and he says, let me go. Jacob, hurt, holding on, answers: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The stranger asks a strange question. What's your name? Jacob. That name carried: the heel-grabber, who came out holding his brother's heel and grabbed a blessing that wasn't his. Then: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel; for thou hast striven with God and with men, and hast prevailed." Yisrael. The first part comes from a Hebrew root meaning to strive, to struggle; the last, el, is God: one who strives with God. Who was the man? The text only says a man. The prophet Hosea calls him an angel. A midrash says he was Esau's own angel, which makes the fight a rehearsal for tomorrow. Jacob names the place Peniel, saying he has seen God face to face and lived. The Torah leaves it open, and the rabbis offer more than one answer. Then the sun rises, and Jacob limps. The blessing doesn't erase the wound; he carries both. The Torah says that's why the children of Israel, to this day, don't eat the sinew of the thigh-vein. And this became the name of a whole people. Not the ones who never doubted, or never argued. The ones who hold on in the dark and won't let go without a blessing. Struggling with God isn't a failure of faith in this story. It's the name.

62.title: The brothers meet (Genesis 33)
62.hook: Esau runs to him, embraces him, and they weep
62.howItsDone: The Mishnah teaches that Yom Kippur does not wipe away a wrong done to another person until that person is appeased, so in the days before it Jews are encouraged to go to the people they have wronged and ask forgiveness directly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yisrael: a night of wrestling, a limp at sunrise, and a new name, one who strives with God. Your line: the struggle is the name.

A rehearsed speech. A gift sent ahead. A careful message to soften the landing. That's how people get ready to face someone they hurt long ago and never made it right with, and Jacob has done all of it. Still limping from the river, he looks up and sees Esau coming, and the four hundred men with him. He lines up his family, the ones he loves most at the very back, and walks out in front. As he comes closer, he bows to the ground, seven times. Years of dread, all in one walk across a field.
screen: `A GIFT SENT AHEAD.` → `FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `SEVEN BOWS.`

segments.voice: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept." Ran. Jacob is inching forward, bowing. Esau runs. The man Jacob feared most closes the distance himself. Then Jacob presses his gifts on him. Esau says, I have enough, my brother; keep what you have. Jacob insists, and uses a telling word. In Hebrew he says: take my blessing. Long ago he took Esau's blessing. Now he's trying to hand one back, and Esau takes it. Look at the page: in a Torah scroll, the Hebrew word for and he kissed him has small dots written over its letters. The rabbis asked why, and they didn't agree. One opinion in the midrash says the dots mean that this once, Esau's kiss was completely from the heart. Another says it wasn't a kiss at all, and reads it darkly. The dots stay on the page, and so do both readings. The ending is honest too. The brothers weep, and then they part. Esau offers to travel together; Jacob politely puts him off and goes his own way. It's not a movie reunion where everyone moves in together. It's two men who were enemies, who cried on each other's necks, and then lived at peace at a distance. Sometimes that's what repair looks like: not everything restored. Just the running, the weeping, and a different road home.

63.title: Dinah (Genesis 34)
63.hook: a hard chapter of violence and revenge that the Torah tells without softening
63.howItsDone: The chapter is read aloud in synagogue each year as part of the weekly Torah portion Vayishlach, and Jewish commentators and modern teachers continue to argue over it rather than explain it away.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayishakehu: Esau ran, they wept, and they went on in peace. Your line: he ran to meet him. This whole week has been Jacob's long road: a switched bride, Leah's sons, Rachel's longing, leaving Laban, the river, and Esau. Today the road gets dark.

A gentle warning first: today is a hard story. If it's too close to home, it's fine to stop here and come back tomorrow. Jacob's family has just made peace with Esau and camped near a city called Shechem. Jacob has a daughter, Dinah, the daughter of Leah. One day she goes out to see the young women of the land. The prince of that city, also named Shechem, sees her, takes her, and violates her. The Torah says it in a few plain words and doesn't look away.
screen: `A HARD CHAPTER.` → `DINAH GOES OUT.` → `THE PRINCE TAKES HER.`

segments.voice: It gets worse. Afterward, the text says, Shechem loves Dinah and wants to marry her, and his father comes to negotiate with Jacob. Jacob stays silent. Dinah's brothers answer, with a trick: every man in your city must be circumcised, and then we'll become one people. The men agree. On the third day, while they're in pain, two of Dinah's brothers, Simeon and Levi, take their swords, walk into the city, and kill every man there. The other brothers plunder it. Jacob finally speaks, and it's about himself: you've made me hated in this land. The brothers get the chapter's last word, a question: "Should one deal with our sister as with a harlot?" Then the story just stops. Nobody resolves it. Readers have argued about it ever since. The great medieval teacher Maimonides wrote that the city deserved its fate, because it failed to bring the prince to justice. Nachmanides answered that this was wrong, and that Jacob was right to be angry. Jacob himself, on his deathbed years later, curses the anger of Simeon and Levi. And notice who never speaks in the whole chapter: Dinah. Men talk about her, bargain for her, kill for her. The Torah never gives us one word from her, or tells us what she felt or wanted. Her name sounds like din, the Hebrew word for judgment, and the story leaves the judgment to us. The Torah could have softened this chapter, or left it out. It didn't.
